proposals.name: Concrete code/data/artifact release commitment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract gives a specific, verifiable commitment to release code/data/models (e.g., a working repository link, an anonymous.4open.science link, a named dataset host, or 'code and data are available at X'). Score 5 if it makes only a vague future promise ('code will be released') with no destination or specificity. Score 0 if there is no mention of code, data, or artifact availability at all.
proposals.rationale: Explicit release links appear constantly in dense_low_card_high rows (R07 'code available at <placeholder>'; R09, R13, R15, R16, R38, R47 all give anonymous.4open.science links; R22 and R32 promise release) but are almost absent from dense_high_card_low rows even when large resources are built (R05's LV3D, R20's HumanVerse have no such line). This suggests the scorecard rewards a reproducibility-signaling boilerplate that the dense reader does not credit.

proposals.name: Fair re-audit of existing methods or benchmarks
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract's central contribution is re-evaluating existing algorithms/models/benchmarks under corrected, fairer, or more systematic conditions and reports how prior claims change as a result. Score 5 if it performs some comparative analysis of existing components without reframing field-level claims. Score 0 if the abstract only proposes a new method with no critical re-examination of prior evaluation validity.
proposals.rationale: R19 (CTBench, re-evaluates certified-training algorithms under fair hyperparameters and shows claimed advantages 'drop significantly') and R35 (JudgeLM, systematically analyzes position/knowledge/format biases in LLM judges) and R56 (comprehensive investigation of CLIP vs. DINO as vision encoders) are all dense_high_card_low, suggesting the dense model rewards this corrective, meta-scientific move much more than the scorecard does.

proposals.name: Human-expert judgment of outputs, not only automatic metrics
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly reports domain-expert or human-annotator evaluation of the method's own outputs (e.g., a stated number of human judges, or a human-labeled benchmark used to validate results/quality). Score 5 if humans are mentioned only for data curation/labeling but not for judging output quality. Score 0 if evaluation is entirely automatic metrics (accuracy, F1, AUC, BLEU, WER, etc.) with no human judgment mentioned.
proposals.rationale: R06 (11 scientists evaluating outputs across correctness/relevance/scientific accuracy) and R54 (human-labeled Visual Abstractions Benchmark used to score reasoning) are dense_high_card_low, while most dense_low_card_high rows (e.g., R27's AUC-ROC, R36's accuracy/kappa) rely purely on automatic metrics.

proposals.name: Theory instantiated as a usable method, not a bound alone
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if a formal theoretical result (proof, guarantee, bound) is explicitly connected to and instantiated as a concrete, usable algorithm or design choice that is then empirically tested. Score 5 if theory and practice are both present but only loosely linked. Score 0 if the contribution is a theoretical result alone with no resulting tested algorithm, or an algorithm with no theoretical grounding at all.
proposals.rationale: R34 (a monotone-improvement guarantee is instantiated as the tested SLBO algorithm) and R40 (a two-layer-network proof backs the tested 'surgical fine-tuning' recipe) are dense_high_card_low, while dense_low_card_high rows like R23 (a generalization bound with no accompanying new algorithm) and R49 (a purely explanatory theoretical account) stop at the theory.

proposals.name: Plain-language explanation of why the mechanism works
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract includes at least one sentence explaining, in intuitive non-jargon terms, why the proposed mechanism should work (e.g., 'we hypothesize that X prevents Y'). Score 5 if the mechanism is named and technically described but its rationale is only implied. Score 0 if the abstract never explains why the method should work, only asserts that it does via reported numbers.
proposals.rationale: R11 ('we hypothesize that randomly masking past tokens prevents over-attending to recent tokens') and R40 ('fine-tuning more parameters on a small target dataset can cause information learned during pre-training to be forgotten') both give a causal, intuitive gloss and are dense_high_card_low; R38's Semantic Field Subspace / Weyl's-theorem description (dense_low_card_high) states mechanism without any such plain-language rationale.

proposals.name: Heterogeneity of evaluation conditions
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the method is evaluated across genuinely different task types, modalities, languages, or domains (e.g., multiple distinct benchmark families, multiple input languages, multiple downstream application types). Score 5 if evaluated on several datasets that are all variants of the same single task/domain. Score 0 if evaluated on only one dataset/benchmark.
proposals.rationale: R05 (outdoor AP-BEV grounding + refCOCO 2D grounding + VQAv2/GQA/SQA/POPE) and R06 (4 languages x 3 comprehension dimensions x 7 models x 11 human judges) show genuinely heterogeneous evaluation and are dense_high_card_low, compared to e.g. R13's single VTAB-1K benchmark (dense_low_card_high).

proposals.name: Scale of a newly constructed resource as a stated contribution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract describes building a new large-scale dataset or benchmark, with a concrete scale figure (image/hour/sample count), that is itself framed as a primary contribution. Score 5 if a new resource is mentioned but its scale/originality is not quantified or emphasized. Score 0 if no new dataset/resource is constructed.
proposals.rationale: R20 (340M-image HumanVerse dataset) and R60 ('largest existing' visual speech dataset, 3,886 hours of video) both foreground the scale of a newly built resource as part of the contribution, and both are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Concrete, named real-world deployment stakes
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract names a specific real-world deployment context or consequential comparison (e.g., a named operational system, a direct comparison to human professional performance, a named application domain with concrete stakes). Score 5 if it gestures at 'real-world applicability' only generically. Score 0 if the work is framed purely as an internal benchmark/metric improvement with no application context.
proposals.rationale: R41 (tested on data from the Curiosity rover currently operating on Mars) and R60 (system's WER compared directly against professional human lipreaders' WER) both anchor the work in a named, concrete deployment or comparison, and both are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Conditional, scoped claims of superiority
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract specifies particular conditions, subsets, or regimes under which the proposed method is better (or worse) than alternatives, rather than claiming uniform dominance. Score 5 if superiority is claimed with a partial hedge ('in most cases'/'on most datasets'). Score 0 if the abstract claims blanket state-of-the-art / superiority everywhere with no scoping.
proposals.rationale: R40 (specifies that fine-tuning only the first few layers works best specifically 'for image corruptions,' implying other shifts favor other subsets) and R56 (specifies CLIP wins at fine-grained/shallow-layer tasks while DINO wins elsewhere) both scope their claims rather than asserting blanket dominance, and both are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Explicitly flagged counterintuitive finding
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly signals that a result defies expectation or prior belief (e.g., 'surprisingly,' 'contrary to,' 'intriguing') and indicates what was expected instead. Score 5 if a notable/unexpected result is reported without being flagged as surprising. Score 0 if all reported findings are presented as expected confirmations of the proposed design.
proposals.rationale: R56 ('Surprisingly, the vision-only model DINO...demonstrates promising performance') and R05 ('CUBE-LLM exhibits intriguing properties similar to LLMs') both explicitly flag an unexpected finding, and both are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Open research question posed before the solution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly frames an unresolved research question or conceptual gap (in question form or a clear gap statement) before presenting the technical solution, with the solution presented as an answer to that question. Score 5 if a gap/limitation is stated but not posed as an actionable question. Score 0 if the abstract moves straight from topic to method with no explicit question or gap framing.
proposals.rationale: R04 ('an interesting question is: would it be more effective to separate highly conflicting objectives...') and R28 ('we study the case in which a trusted...verifier can learn to interact with...provers') both open with an explicit unresolved question/framing before the method, and both are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Quantitative results interpreted, not just listed
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if quantitative results are woven into explanatory sentences that state what the number means for the paper's claim (e.g., 'reconstructs the score with X% error, showing Y'). Score 5 if numbers are reported with only light surrounding context. Score 0 if the abstract is dominated by a bare list of percentages/multipliers with no interpretive sentence connecting them to the claim.
proposals.rationale: R03 (each RMSE/correlation figure is tied to an explanatory clause about what it demonstrates about underlying abilities) and R01 (BLEU numbers are framed narratively as 'records' rather than a bare list) both interpret their numbers and are dense_high_card_low, contrasting with denser bare-statistic listings in rows like R36 and R38 (dense_low_card_high).

proposals.name: Cross-field grounding of the approach
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly draws on and names concepts/techniques from more than one distinct field (e.g., complexity/game theory plus deep learning, planetary robotics plus reinforcement learning) to justify or construct the method. Score 5 if a single borrowed concept from another field is mentioned only in passing. Score 0 if the approach and its motivation are framed entirely within one subfield's own vocabulary.
proposals.rationale: R28 (builds on prover-verifier games from game/complexity theory to construct neural interactive proofs for AI safety) and R41 (grounds value-iteration RL in planetary robotics/Mars rover navigation) both explicitly ground the method in a second field, and both are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Specific mechanism of baseline failure identified
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract names a precise, mechanistic failure mode of prior/existing approaches (what specifically goes wrong and why) rather than a generic limitation. Score 5 if a limitation is named but not explained mechanistically. Score 0 if prior work is only described as 'limited,' 'underexplored,' or 'insufficient' with no specifics.
proposals.rationale: R20 (names the specific failure that existing models 'generate human images with incoherent parts or unnatural poses') and R57 (names catastrophic forgetting specifically as the failure mode when injecting multiple kinds of knowledge) both give a precise failure mechanism, and both are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Abstract reads as one coherent argument, not a fragment list
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract flows as one integrated narrative (problem, insight, method, validation) with clear logical connectives. Score 5 if it is readable but reads as a loosely connected sequence of claims. Score 0 if it reads as a fragmented list of disconnected technical assertions/results, or relies on gimmicks such as spelling out an acronym letter-by-letter in place of plain description.
proposals.rationale: R38 (spells out 'SAFARI' letter-by-letter inline via typeset emphasis on each letter) and R53 (reads as a sequence of short, disconnected declarative lines rather than a flowing argument) both show fragmented/gimmicky presentation and are dense_low_card_high, while dense_high_card_low rows like R20 and R54 read as single flowing arguments.

proposals.name: Expectation-violating finding stated with its scope condition
proposals.instruction: Score how much the abstract reports a specific claim that cuts against a reasonable default expectation in its subfield, together with the condition under which that claim holds. 10 = a clearly identified surprise plus its boundary, stated concretely enough that a reader could try to falsify it (e.g. a component widely assumed necessary turns out unnecessary; or which of two choices wins flips depending on a named factor). 5 = a mild or partial surprise, or a surprise asserted with no condition attached. 0 = nothing in the abstract could have come out otherwise; it reports only that the proposed method beats prior methods on the usual benchmarks.
proposals.rationale: R45 reports that a vision-only model (DINO) beats CLIP for fine-grained perception and that shallow CLIP layers, not deep ones, help grounding - a live surprise with a named regime; R11 reports that WHICH layers to fine-tune flips with the TYPE of distribution shift; R03 reports that pure data scaling yields 3D perception with no 3D-specific architecture; R43 reports that recent algorithms lose their claimed advantage once baselines are fairly tuned. All four sit high on dense and low on card, suggesting the scorecard has no slot for a claim that carries risk of being wrong.

proposals.name: Headline result anchored to an externally interpretable reference point
proposals.instruction: Score whether the main quantitative result is placed against a reference a reader outside this paper can independently interpret. 10 = the result is stated against human performance, a published record on a named dataset, a competition outcome, or a specific named prior system with ITS number also given. 5 = numbers on named benchmarks but compared only to generic baselines or unnamed prior work. 0 = improvement expressed only as outperforms baselines / achieves state of the art, with no interpretable anchor.
proposals.rationale: R38 gives 40.9 percent WER against professional lipreaders at 86.4 and 92.9 percent on the same data, and against named prior systems at 89.8 and 76.8; R02 gives 35.44 BLEU on IWSLT14 and 31.03 on WMT14 as records with the delta over a named strong Transformer baseline; R09 cites a KDD Cup winning entry on a graph orders of magnitude larger than prior benchmarks. Contrast R49 (state of the art on most of thirteen datasets, no anchor) and R31 (outperforms seven baselines by notable margins) which score high on card and low on dense.

proposals.name: Contribution removes a requirement rather than adding a part
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the central contribution is subtractive: something previously treated as necessary is shown to be unnecessary, and the abstract names both what is dropped and what is retained. 10 = an explicit elimination (no negative examples needed, no architectural change needed, no hand-engineered features needed, no explicit uncertainty quantification needed) that is the paper's main claim. 5 = a simplification mentioned as a side benefit. 0 = purely additive: new modules, losses, or stages stacked onto an existing pipeline.
proposals.rationale: R09 eliminates negative examples and complex augmentations; R20 extends optimism-under-uncertainty in a way that requires no explicit uncertainty quantification; R51 requires virtually no architectural change from the baseline network; R57 removes manual paralinguistic feature selection. These are dense-high / card-low. Contrast the card-high, dense-low R36 and R29, whose contributions are enumerations of added components.

proposals.name: Explicit mechanism given for why the method should work
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract states a causal account of why the proposed change helps, specific enough to be wrong. 10 = a named mechanism or diagnosis (this fails because of X, so we do Y, which removes X), including hypotheses flagged as such. 5 = a vague gesture at intuition (leverages richer information, better captures structure). 0 = the method is described only procedurally and its effectiveness is established purely by results.
proposals.rationale: R34 states the hypothesis that masking random past tokens prevents over-attending to recent tokens; R05 derives that vanilla HLR suffers a mismatch between refined Gaussian conditional and hyperprior distributions and fixes exactly that; R11 gives the forgetting account plus a two-layer proof; R60 states the multi-granularity structural insight as the reason for joint denoising. All dense-high / card-low. R49 and R36 (dense-low / card-high) describe components and results with no why.

proposals.name: Claimed virtues tied to evidence rather than stacked as adjectives
proposals.instruction: Score how tightly each desirable property claimed is bound to a specific measurement, dataset, or argument. 10 = every claimed property (accuracy, speed, robustness, generalization, scalability) is attached to something checkable. 5 = a mix, with some properties asserted bare. 0 = a run of virtues asserted in a single breath, none of them attached to a number, a condition, or a mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R49 closes with high accuracy, rapid convergence, robustness across varying dataset complexities, and strong generalization in both transductive and inductive settings, none quantified; R31 says consistently outperforms by notable margins; R17 says strong baseline and carefully designed prompts. All three are card-high / dense-low, consistent with a scorecard that credits the presence of a virtue-word rather than its backing.

proposals.name: Absence of promotional self-description
proposals.instruction: Score the neutrality of the language the abstract uses about ITS OWN contribution. 10 = contribution described in flat, checkable terms; the reader is left to judge significance. 5 = occasional mild boosterism (novel, effective) alongside substance. 0 = self-applied superlatives doing the work evidence should do (breakthrough, innovative, first-ever, whistleblower, remarkable). Enthusiasm about the field or about prior work is NOT penalized; only self-praise.
proposals.rationale: R15 calls its own contribution the breakthrough; R22 says its research acts as a whistleblower for the community; R17 introduces an innovative task for the first time and a strong baseline. These are card-high / dense-low. The dense-high side is conspicuously plain: R06 frames itself as an investigation with an open question, and R26 offers early training results.

proposals.name: One load-bearing idea versus bolted-together named components
proposals.instruction: Score whether the contribution is a single idea carried through, or an assembly. 10 = one mechanism, developed and tested; any sub-parts are shown to be facets of that one mechanism. 5 = a main idea with one auxiliary trick. 0 = the contribution IS an enumeration of two or more separately named or acronymed modules whose only stated relationship is that they are used together, or a laundry list of independent additions.
proposals.rationale: R36 is IKL = IUR + ICL, two independently motivated pieces; R52 pairs subgoal construction with a diffusion model for demonstration ordering, two unrelated literatures; R29 stacks a CRNN-TA architecture, a grad-CAM adaptation, a shuffled-crossover augmentation, and an attention-based trial-rejection loop. All card-high / dense-low. Contrast R07 (two contributions that are both about step count) and R11 (one idea).

proposals.name: Relative gains reported with absolute base and measurement conditions
proposals.instruction: Score whether relative claims can be reconstructed by the reader. 10 = every fold-change, percentage, or speedup is accompanied by the absolute quantity it is relative to and the setting it was measured in (model, hardware, dataset, baseline identity). 5 = some anchored, some floating. 0 = large relative numbers with no base value, no setting, and no identified comparator.
proposals.rationale: R53 claims up to 384 percent faster sampling and 1822 percent reduced memory with no base, no hardware, and no named comparator; R37 claims a 15 to 30 times speedup similarly unanchored. Both are card-high / dense-low: a scorecard sees big numbers, a careful reader sees uninterpretable ones. Contrast R34 (55.7 to 59.2 on SuperGLUE), R07 (1024 or 8192 steps down to 4, FID 3.0 on CIFAR-10), and R21 (3x memory reduction at 9 to 16 percent compute overhead), which are reconstructable.

proposals.name: Definite claim paired with an acknowledged limit
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract states a boundary on its own result while still committing to a claim. 10 = a clear positive claim plus an explicit limit: where it does not hold, what remains unsolved, that results are preliminary, or a reported failure of the thing being studied. 5 = a hedge with no specific content. 0 = uniformly positive; consistent superiority everywhere, no stated boundary, no negative finding.
proposals.rationale: R26 presents early training results on Curiosity rover data while still claiming the method works; R54 reports that ALL models including its best perform poorly on complex prompts; R43 reports that the field's claimed gains shrink under fair evaluation; R06 declines a superiority claim and reports which objectives conflict. All dense-high or dense-mid with low card. The card-high side (R49, R31, R58) is uniformly and unboundedly positive.

proposals.name: Motivation names a specific defect of the current best approach
proposals.instruction: Score how concrete and attributable the stated gap is. 10 = the motivation is a named failure mode of a named existing method or family, with an account of HOW it fails (this method degrades in this regime, for this reason). 5 = a real but generic limitation of a family of approaches. 0 = field-level throat clearing: the area is important, challenges remain, existing work is limited.
proposals.rationale: R05 names hybrid latent refinement and the exact cross-domain rate degradation it exhibits; R45 names reliance on CLIP deep-layer features and the missing analysis; R57 names the insufficiency of pitch features and the hand-engineering they require; R04 names the editability-versus-personalization trade-off. All dense-high / card-low. Contrast R44 (open-source environments have not advanced and are often toy scenarios) and R37 (their abstract nature and computational complexity remain significant challenges), both card-high / dense-low.

proposals.name: Formal result paired with an experiment that could disconfirm it
proposals.instruction: Score the coupling between theory and evidence. 10 = a stated formal result AND experiments whose design follows from it, so the experiment is a test of the theory and not merely a separate benchmark table. 5 = theory and experiments both present but logically unconnected. 0 = a guarantee invoked with no stated content (we provide theoretical guarantees) and/or experiments that bear on a different claim than the theory does.
proposals.rationale: R01 gives a theoretical comparison of protocols and then a toy graph-isomorphism domain chosen to illustrate the key ideas plus a realistic code-validation task; R11 proves first-layer tuning can beat full tuning in an idealized model and then tests exactly the shift-type prediction across seven tasks; R20 proves monotone improvement for a meta-algorithm and instantiates it as SLBO. All dense-high / card-low. Contrast R58 (theoretical guarantees of convergence to a near-optimal mask, then a benchmark comparison that tests nothing of the sort) and R33 (many loosely stitched theoretical claims), both card-high / dense-low.

proposals.name: Consequence extends beyond the proposed method
proposals.instruction: Score whether, if the paper's claim were true, researchers who never adopt this particular method would have to change what they do. 10 = the finding revises how a task should be measured, how baselines should be built, or what a whole family of methods can be assumed to need. 5 = useful to a specific subfield's practitioners. 0 = the claim's consequences are confined to users of this exact method or artifact.
proposals.rationale: R46 shows six standard benchmarks are compressible to under 3 percent of their items with one dominant factor, which bears on anyone who reports those benchmarks; R43 shows reported gains in certified training shrink under fair tuning; R11 changes default fine-tuning practice; R01 sets a shared framework generalizing prior protocols. All dense-high / card-low. Contrast R19 (an iteration schedule for one attack generator) and R27 (a hyperparameter setting for random forests), card-high / dense-very-low.

proposals.name: Information density: content per sentence
proposals.instruction: Score the fraction of sentences that carry a specific fact, quantity, mechanism, or falsifiable claim. 10 = nearly every sentence adds content; the abstract reaches its actual contribution within the first two sentences. 5 = a conventional two-sentence setup followed by dense content. 0 = a long motivational preamble about the importance of the area, plus a closing aspiration (we hope to inspire, paving the way), with the actual contribution occupying a small minority of the text.
proposals.rationale: R44 spends roughly half its length on ecological-importance framing and closes on we hope to advance and inspire; R58 opens on LLMs enhancing various aspects of our daily lives from conversational AI to search; R22 closes on whistleblowing and advocacy. All card-high / dense-low. Contrast R30 and R07, which state the contribution in sentence one or two and spend the remainder on specifics, both dense-high / card-low.

proposals.name: Comparison integrity: baselines treated as tunable, not fixed
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract shows awareness that its comparison could be unfair and says what was done about it. 10 = explicit protocol control: baselines re-tuned or upgraded, matched training schedules, matched evaluation method, a named strong baseline reported with its own number, or identified and mitigated evaluation biases. 5 = comparison to recognized strong baselines without discussion of tuning. 0 = the count of baselines or datasets is offered as the entire evidence of rigor.
proposals.rationale: R43 is built on this criterion (fair schedule, fair certification, systematically tuned hyperparameters, and the finding that this erases claimed advantages) and is dense-high / card-low; R02 names the strong Transformer baseline and gives the 2.6 BLEU delta over it; R25 identifies position, knowledge, and format bias in its own instrument and mitigates each. Contrast R31 (seven baselines, 19 datasets, notable margins) and R49 (thirteen datasets), where breadth substitutes for fairness, both card-high / dense-low.

proposals.name: Released artifact described with scientific substance, not just linked
proposals.instruction: Score how well any dataset, benchmark, or code release is characterized in the abstract itself. 10 = scale, composition, coverage, and what the artifact makes possible are stated, so a reader can judge its value without downloading it. 5 = named and linked, with partial description. 0 = a bare anonymized URL, or a promise contingent on acceptance or publication, with no description of what the artifact contains.
proposals.rationale: R38 specifies 3,886 hours of paired video and text and the pipeline stages it supports; R03 specifies how LV3D was assembled from existing 2D and 3D datasets under a common multi-turn QA formulation; R55 specifies modalities, languages, tasks, and two benchmark protocols; these carry real information. Contrast R21, R36, and R52, whose release is contingent (available upon acceptance / open-sourced upon publication), and R31 and R37, which supply a bare anonymous link - all card-high / dense-low, which is what a scorecard crediting artifact availability as a checkbox would produce.

proposals.name: Problem–mechanism fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the proposed mechanism directly addresses a specifically diagnosed bottleneck and the abstract explains why; score 0 when the method is weakly connected to a generic problem statement.
proposals.rationale: The tight diagnosis-to-mechanism links in R07 and R43 contrast with more generic improvement claims in R10 and R25.

proposals.name: Non-obvious conceptual synthesis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work combines ideas from distinct areas into a clearly motivated, non-trivial principle; score 0 when it mainly concatenates familiar modules without a new conceptual connection.
proposals.rationale: R15 connects binary-network behavior to high-dimensional geometry, while R46 unifies neural interactive-proof protocols; these contrasts with routine component combinations such as R31.

proposals.name: Mechanistic novelty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a genuinely new operation, representation, or learning mechanism whose role is clear; score 0 when novelty is only a renamed architecture or a minor parameter change.
proposals.rationale: The structural denoising mechanism in R17 and progressive sampling construction in R51 show concrete mechanism-level novelty, unlike the more incremental presentation in R32.

proposals.name: Scope under meaningful variation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when evaluation deliberately varies domains, tasks, shifts, scales, or deployment settings that test the claimed scope; score 0 when evidence comes from one narrow, convenient setting.
proposals.rationale: R16 varies objectives, languages, datasets, and tasks, and R38 tests discretizations, noise, and PDE orders; narrow benchmark claims appear in R23 and R50.

proposals.name: Comparison fairness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when baselines, tuning, schedules, metrics, and compute are explicitly made comparable; score 0 when superiority is asserted without credible control of comparison conditions.
proposals.rationale: R22 explicitly exposes unfair historical comparisons, while R30 and R56 provide concrete competitive reference points; several scorecard-favored abstracts merely claim state of the art, such as R10 and R25.

proposals.name: Quantified efficiency–quality tradeoff
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract quantifies both resource savings and the resulting accuracy, quality, or capability cost; score 0 when efficiency or performance is only described qualitatively.
proposals.rationale: R04, R13, and R57 quantify speed or memory together with performance, whereas R53 makes broad efficiency claims with less concrete tradeoff detail.

proposals.name: Theory–algorithm correspondence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a stated theorem or analysis directly motivates the algorithm and predicts an observable behavior tested experimentally; score 0 when theory and experiments are disconnected or theory is merely decorative.
proposals.rationale: R58 turns a lower-bound guarantee into an optimization framework, and R05 links stability bounds to momentum; R50 presents many theoretical claims without an equally clear empirical correspondence.

proposals.name: Diagnostic evidence of causality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when ablations, controlled variants, or targeted analyses isolate which design choice causes the improvement; score 0 when the abstract reports only aggregate end-to-end gains.
proposals.rationale: R12 tests the masking hypothesis and R41 compares encoder layers and feature sources, while R10 and R31 mostly report overall superiority.

proposals.name: Transfer beyond the training regime
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method demonstrably transfers across unseen objects, domains, tasks, or distributions central to the claim; score 0 when evaluation remains within the same narrow regime used to motivate training.
proposals.rationale: R06 evaluates newly encountered shapes and R49 adapts without source-data access; single-family evaluations such as R23 and R32 provide weaker transfer evidence.

proposals.name: Benchmark or dataset utility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a new benchmark or dataset measures an important, previously missing capability with coverage, task design, and baselines that enable meaningful future comparison; score 0 when it is merely a collection of routine examples or lacks evidence of usefulness.
proposals.rationale: R03 decomposes scientific-image understanding into specific dimensions and languages, and R60 targets realistic multi-agent ecological tasks; R34 contributes data but offers less evidence about breadth of downstream utility.

proposals.name: Evaluation–claim alignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the metrics and test tasks directly measure the paper’s central capability and avoid known leakage or proxy failures; score 0 when headline metrics are poorly matched to the stated objective.
proposals.rationale: R42 explicitly removes uninformative and leaky samples, and R09 analyzes judge biases; abstracts relying on generic benchmark scores for broad claims, such as R31 and R39, are more vulnerable to over-credit.

proposals.name: Operational realism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract specifies realistic constraints, inputs, failure modes, or deployment conditions and shows the method addresses them; score 0 when the application framing is aspirational with no operational constraints.
proposals.rationale: R02 uses rover data and navigation constraints, while R34 addresses scarce invasive brain recordings; broad application language in R60 and R39 is less technically operationalized.

proposals.name: Failure-mode awareness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies important limitations or failure modes and tests how the method behaves under them; score 0 when it presents only unconditional success language.
proposals.rationale: R03 explicitly reports failures on complex scientific-image prompts, and R22 reveals that claimed advantages collapse under fair tuning; unconditional claims appear in R10 and R25.

proposals.name: Explanatory insight
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work explains why a phenomenon occurs or why the method succeeds in a way that generalizes beyond the immediate experiment; score 0 when it offers only performance improvement without explanation.
proposals.rationale: R01 explains distributional-RL gains through risk-sensitive entropy, and R15 explains binary-network learning geometrically; purely empirical abstracts such as R23 and R32 provide little such insight.

proposals.name: Implementation specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract makes the method sufficiently concrete to reconstruct its essential data flow, training procedure, and evaluation protocol; score 0 when the proposal is dominated by slogans, unexplained acronyms, or vague claims.
proposals.rationale: R47 clearly specifies receptive tokens, masks, losses, and teacher handling, while R18 explains Binder’s parsing and execution stages; dense but underspecified descriptions such as R34 and R39 risk scorecard over-credit.

proposals.name: Causal mechanism clarity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract clearly connects a specific limitation to a concrete design choice and then to the claimed effect; score 0 when it mainly lists components and results without explaining why they should work.
proposals.rationale: R06 and R55 articulate unusually clear limitation-to-mechanism chains, whereas R16 and R60 present dense technical claims with weaker causal explanation.

proposals.name: Bottleneck-to-solution fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when every major method component directly addresses a well-defined bottleneck under the stated setting; score 0 when the proposed technique is only loosely related to the motivating problem.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R58 tightly match their architectures to scalability and irregular-observation constraints, while R48 and R45 provide less convincing alignment between motivation and intervention.

proposals.name: Conceptual reframe
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work introduces a genuinely new way to formulate, represent, or reason about the problem; score 0 when it is primarily a routine module, tuning change, or renamed combination of familiar techniques.
proposals.rationale: R07, R43, and R55 each introduce a distinctive conceptual framing, while R23 and R48 read more like collections of incremental components.

proposals.name: Constraint-aware efficiency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a practical resource, data, latency, or privacy constraint and quantifies a favorable accuracy-quality tradeoff; score 0 when efficiency is asserted only vaguely or is unrelated to the central contribution.
proposals.rationale: R06, R24, and R47 connect algorithm design to explicit compute or memory savings, unlike the largely generic efficiency language in R02 and R14.

proposals.name: Cross-setting stress coverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method is tested across substantially varied datasets, domains, modalities, or task conditions that probe the stated claim; score 0 when evidence comes from one narrow or homogeneous setting.
proposals.rationale: R03, R19, and R58 test broad variations that directly probe generality, whereas R17 and R45 rely on much narrower empirical settings.

proposals.name: Failure-mode diagnosis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when experiments or analysis isolate specific failure modes, biases, or component effects and use them to explain improvements; score 0 when the abstract reports only aggregate performance.
proposals.rationale: R08, R09, and R30 explicitly analyze fairness, objective conflicts, or encoder behavior, while R14 and R48 emphasize performance without comparable diagnosis.

proposals.name: Benchmark ecosystem value
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a dataset or benchmark has clearly defined coverage, challenging evaluation dimensions, useful baselines, and a stated research purpose; score 0 when it merely announces data or environments without showing why they enable better science.
proposals.rationale: R10, R36, and R52 describe purpose-built resources with task coverage and baselines, while R49 gives less evidence that its reduced benchmark captures the relevant capabilities.

proposals.name: Theory-to-algorithm coupling
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the theoretical result directly motivates the algorithm or its guarantee and the experiments test that connection; score 0 when theory and empirical method are presented as largely independent claims.
proposals.rationale: R06, R38, and R55 connect formal analyses to concrete algorithmic choices, whereas R17 and R60 provide theory with comparatively little mechanism-specific empirical validation.

proposals.name: Quantitative claim specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when gains are reported with concrete metrics, baselines, datasets, scales, and relevant conditions; score 0 when the abstract relies mostly on unqualified phrases such as substantial or state of the art.
proposals.rationale: R26, R28, and R57 provide precise comparative numbers and operating conditions, while R14 and R48 make broader claims with fewer anchoring details.

proposals.name: Transferable capability evidence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract demonstrates that the learned capability transfers to new objects, domains, task types, or deployment conditions beyond the training formulation; score 0 when performance is shown only on the directly optimized task.
proposals.rationale: R19, R22, and R34 provide evidence of transfer across 3D contexts, objects, or distribution shifts, unlike the more task-local evidence in R27 and R45.

proposals.name: Fair comparative design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when comparisons use strong, clearly matched baselines across multiple controlled settings and distinguish algorithmic effects from tuning or protocol effects; score 0 when comparisons are narrow, ambiguous, or vulnerable to unfair baselines.
proposals.rationale: R08 explicitly controls training schedules and certification procedures, and R26 compares against several optimization tools, whereas R14 and R48 give less evidence of comparative control.

proposals.name: Claim-scope discipline
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when conclusions are carefully limited to the demonstrated settings and conditions, with dependencies or limitations made clear; score 0 when narrow evidence is used to support sweeping claims about broad capability or safety.
proposals.rationale: R08 and R34 qualify their conclusions by specifying conditions and sources of variation, while R02 and R36 make expansive claims extending well beyond the concrete evidence summarized.

proposals.name: Reproduction-ready detail
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract specifies the inputs, principal operations, training or inference procedure, evaluation setting, and relevant scale well enough to reconstruct the contribution conceptually; score 0 when the method remains opaque despite technical terminology.
proposals.rationale: R06, R41, and R46 provide unusually concrete descriptions of inputs, modules, and evaluation scale, while R29 and R60 leave key operational details unspecified.

proposals.name: Practical consequence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the target problem has a concrete scientific, societal, or deployment consequence and the proposed method addresses that consequence directly; score 0 when the task is presented mainly as an abstract benchmark exercise with no demonstrated relevance.
proposals.rationale: R05, R57, and R58 tie their problems to realistic generation, communication, or physical-system applications, whereas R45 and R48 offer less compelling downstream significance.

proposals.name: End-to-end integration coherence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when multiple components form a complementary pipeline whose interactions are necessary for the claimed capability; score 0 when the abstract presents an arbitrary bundle of techniques with no explanation of how they work together.
proposals.rationale: R05, R20, and R41 describe components that jointly support a coherent end-to-end capability, while R23 and R32 provide weaker evidence that their named components form an integrated mechanism.
